{{Short description|Theorem describing translation of Gaussian measures on Hilbert spaces}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Cameron–Martin theorem''' or '''Cameron–Martin formula''' (named after [[Robert Horton Cameron]] and [[W. T. Martin]]) is a [[theorem]] of [[measure theory]] that describes how [[Abstract Wiener space|abstract Wiener measure]] changes under [[Translation (geometry)|translation]] by certain elements of the Cameron–Martin [[Hilbert space]].

==Motivation==

The standard [[Gaussian measure]] <math>\gamma^n</math> on <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\mathbf{R}^n</math> is not translation-[[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]].  (In fact, there is a unique translation invariant [[Radon measure]] up to scale by [[Haar's theorem]]: the <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Lebesgue measure]], denoted here <math>dx</math>.)  Instead, a measurable subset <math>A</math> has [[Gaussian measure]]

:<math>\gamma_n(A) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\int_A \exp\left(-\tfrac12\langle x, x\rangle_{\mathbf R^n}\right)\,dx.</math>

Here <math>\langle x,x\rangle_{\mathbf R^n}</math> refers to the standard Euclidean [[dot product]] in <math>\mathbf{R}^n</math>.  The Gaussian measure of the translation of <math>A</math> by a vector <math>h \in \mathbf{R}^n</math> is

:<math>\begin{align}
\gamma_n(A-h) &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\int_A \exp\left(-\tfrac12\langle x-h, x-h\rangle_{\mathbf R^n}\right)\,dx\\[4pt]
&=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}}\int_A \exp\left(\frac{2\langle x, h\rangle_{\mathbf R^n} - \langle h, h\rangle_{\mathbf R^n}}{2}\right)\exp\left(-\tfrac12\langle x, x\rangle_{\mathbf R^n}\right)\,dx.
\end{align}</math>

So under translation through <math>h</math>, the Gaussian measure scales by the distribution function appearing in the last display:

:<math>\exp\left(\frac{2\langle x, h\rangle_{\mathbf R^n} - \langle h, h\rangle_{\mathbf R^n}}{2} \right)=\exp\left(\langle x, h\rangle_{\mathbf R^n} - \tfrac12\|h\|_{\mathbf R^n}^ 2\right).</math>

The measure that associates to the set <math>A</math> the number <math>\gamma_n(A - h)</math> is the [[pushforward measure]], denoted <math>(T_h)_* (\gamma^n).</math>  Here <math>T_h : \mathbf{R}^n \to \mathbf{R}^n</math> refers to the translation map: <math>T_h(x) = x + h</math>.  The above calculation shows that the [[Radon–Nikodym derivative]] of the pushforward measure with respect to the original Gaussian measure is given by

:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d} (T_h)_{*} (\gamma^n)}{\mathrm{d} \gamma^n} (x) = \exp \left( \left \langle h, x \right \rangle_{\mathbf{R}^n} - \tfrac{1}{2} \| h \|_{\mathbf{R}^n}^2 \right).</math>

The abstract Wiener measure <math>\gamma</math> on a [[separable space|separable]] [[Banach space]] <math>E</math>, where <math>i : H \to E</math> is an [[abstract Wiener space]], is also a "Gaussian measure" in a suitable sense. How does it change under translation? It turns out that a similar formula to the one above holds if we consider only translations by elements of the [[Dense set|dense]] [[linear subspace|subspace]] <math>i(H) \subseteq E</math>.

==Statement of the theorem==

=== For abstract Wiener spaces (Banach space setting) ===
Let <math>i : H \to E</math> be an abstract Wiener space with abstract Wiener measure <math>\gamma : \operatorname{Borel}(E) \to [0, 1]</math>. For <math>h \in H</math>, define <math>T_h : E \to E</math> by <math>T_h(x) = x + i(h)</math>. Then <math>(T_h)_*(\gamma)</math> is [[Equivalence (measure theory)|equivalent]] to <math>\gamma</math> with Radon–Nikodym derivative

:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d} (T_{h})_{*} (\gamma)}{\mathrm{d} \gamma} (x) = \exp \left( \langle h, x \rangle^{\sim} - \tfrac{1}{2} \| h \|_{H}^{2} \right),</math>

where

:<math>\langle h, x \rangle^{\sim} = i(h) (x)</math>

denotes the [[Paley–Wiener integral]].

The Cameron–Martin formula is valid only for translations by elements of the dense subspace <math>i(H) \subseteq E</math>, called '''Cameron–Martin space''', and not by arbitrary elements of <math>E</math>. If the Cameron–Martin formula did hold for arbitrary translations, it would contradict the following result:

:If <math>E</math> is a separable Banach space and <math>\mu</math> is a locally finite [[Borel measure]] on <math>E</math> that is equivalent to its own push forward under any translation, then either <math>E</math> has finite dimension or <math>\mu</math> is the [[trivial measure|trivial (zero) measure]]. (See [[quasi-invariant measure]].)

In fact, <math>\gamma</math> is quasi-invariant under translation by an element <math>v</math> [[if and only if]] <math>v \in i(H)</math>. Vectors in <math>i(H)</math> are sometimes known as '''Cameron–Martin directions'''.

=== General version for locally convex vector spaces ===
Consider a [[locally convex vector space]] <math>E</math>, with a Gaussian measure <math>\gamma</math> on the [[cylindrical σ-algebra]] <math>\sigma(\operatorname{Cyl}(E,E'))</math> and let <math>\gamma_{m}:=\gamma(\cdot - m)</math> denote the translation by <math>m\in E</math>. For an element in the topological dual <math>f\in E'</math> define the distance to the mean <math>t_{\gamma}(f):=f-\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}[f],</math>
and denote the closure in <math>L^2(E,\gamma)</math> as <math>E_a^{\gamma}:=\operatorname{clos}\left\{(t_{\gamma}(f_n))_{n}\colon\ f\in E'\right\}</math>.
Define the covariance operator <math>\overline{R_{\gamma}}:E_a^{\gamma}\to (E')^*</math> extended to the closure as
:<math>\overline{R_{\gamma}}(f)(g)=\langle f,g-\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}[g]\rangle_{L^2(\gamma)}</math>.

Define the norm 
:<math>\|h\|_{H_\gamma}:=\sup\{f(h)\colon f\in E',\; \overline{R_{\gamma}}(f)(f) \leq 1\},</math>
then the '''Cameron–Martin space''' <math>H_\gamma</math> of <math>\gamma</math> in <math>E</math> is 
:<math>H_\gamma=\{h\in E\colon \|h\|_{H_\gamma}<\infty\}</math>.
If for <math>h\in E</math> there exists an <math>g\in E_a^{\gamma}</math> such that <math>h=\overline{R_{\gamma}}(g)</math> then <math>h\in H_\gamma</math> and <math>\|h\|_{H_\gamma} = \|g\|_{L^2(\gamma)}</math>. Further there is [[Equivalence (measure theory)|equivalence]] <math>\gamma_h \sim \gamma</math> with Radon-Nikodým density
::<math>\frac{d\gamma_h}{d\gamma}=\exp\left(g(x)-\frac{1}{2}\|h\|_{H_\gamma}^2\right).</math>
If <math>h\not\in H_\gamma</math> the two measures are [[singular measure|singular]].<ref>{{cite book |first1=Vladimir |last1=Bogachev| publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|title=Gaussian Measures|place=Rhode Island|date=1998}}</ref>

==Integration by parts==

The Cameron–Martin formula gives rise to an [[integration by parts]] formula on <math>E</math>: if <math>F : E \to \mathbf{R}</math>  has [[Bounded function|bounded]] [[Fréchet derivative]] <math>\mathrm{D}F : E \to \operatorname{Lin}(E; \mathbf{R}) = E^*</math>, integrating the Cameron–Martin formula with respect to Wiener measure on both sides gives

:<math>\int_{E} F(x + t i(h)) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x) = \int_{E} F(x) \exp \left( t \langle h, x \rangle^{\sim} - \tfrac{1}{2} t^2 \| h \|_{H}^{2} \right) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x)</math>

for any <math>t \in \mathbf{R}</math>. Formally differentiating with respect to <math>t</math> and evaluating at <math>t = 0</math> gives the integration by parts formula

:<math>\int_E \mathrm{D} F(x) (i(h)) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x) = \int_E F(x) \langle h, x \rangle^\sim \, \mathrm{d} \gamma (x).</math>

Comparison with the [[divergence theorem]] of [[vector calculus]] suggests

:<math>\mathop{\mathrm{div}} [V_h] (x) = - \langle h, x \rangle^\sim,</math>

where <math>V_h : E \to E</math> is the constant "[[vector field]]" <math>V_h(x) = i(h)</math> for all <math>x \in E</math>. The wish to consider more general vector fields and to think of stochastic integrals as "divergences" leads to the study of [[stochastic processes]] and the [[Malliavin calculus]], and, in particular, the [[Clark–Ocone theorem]] and its associated integration by parts formula.

==An application==

Using Cameron–Martin theorem one may establish (See Liptser and Shiryayev 1977, p.&nbsp;280) that for a <math>q \times q</math> symmetric non-negative [[Definiteness of a matrix|definite matrix]] <math>H(t)</math> whose elements <math>H_{j, k}(t)</math> are continuous and satisfy the condition

:<math> \int_0^T \sum_{j,k=1} ^q |H_{j,k}(t)|\,dt < \infty, </math>

it holds for a <math>q</math>−dimensional [[Wiener process]] <math>w(t)</math> that

:<math> E \left[ \exp \left( -\int_0^T w(t)^*H(t)w(t) \, dt \right) \right] = \exp \left[ \tfrac{1}{2} \int_0^T \operatorname{tr} (G(t)) \, dt \right], </math>

where <math>G(t)</math> is a <math>q \times q</math> nonpositive definite matrix which is a unique solution of the matrix-valued [[Riccati differential equation]]

:<math> \frac{dG(t)}{dt} = 2H(t)-G^2(t)</math>

with the boundary condition <math>G(T) = 0</math>.

In the special case of a one-dimensional Brownian motion where <math>H(t)=1/2</math>, the unique solution is <math>G(t)=\tanh(t-T)</math>, and we have the original formula as established by Cameron and Martin:
<math display="block">E\left[\exp\left(-\tfrac12\int_0^T w(t)^2\,dt\right)\right] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\cosh T}}.</math>
